q: A team has 2 services on one small rented server and 200 users. Which option is the right size?
options: Kubernetes, so they are ready to grow
Docker Compose, or CapRover if they want a dashboard and automatic HTTPS
AWS Lambda, because it needs no server
A cluster of five servers
why: Pick the smallest option that solves today's problem. Kubernetes adds a lot to learn and run, and gives nothing extra at this size.

q: Which two options mean YOU look after the machines, and which of the two can use more than one machine?
options: Compose and CapRover. Only CapRover (built on Swarm) can use more than one machine
Lambda and Fargate. Only Fargate can use more than one machine
Kubernetes and Lambda. Only Kubernetes
A hosted platform and Fargate. Both
why: On Compose and CapRover you rent and patch the servers. Compose controls one Docker engine, so it stays on one machine. CapRover rides on Swarm.

q: A team runs 5 copies of an API with Compose on one server. The server dies. What happens?
options: Compose starts the copies on another server
Only one copy dies, the other four carry on
All 5 copies die, because they were all on one machine
Nothing, Compose keeps a backup
why: Copies on one machine are not safety. To spread copies and replace them on other machines you need an orchestrator such as Swarm, ECS or Kubernetes.

q: What do Swarm (so CapRover), ECS and Kubernetes have in common that Compose lacks?
options: They all use YAML
They keep a desired count of copies alive with a loop that compares what you want with what is running
They only run on AWS
They need no containers
why: You say how many copies you want. The loop starts or stops copies to make it true, and a crashed copy is replaced on the next pass.

q: A job runs for 25 minutes and needs 2 GB of memory. Is plain AWS Lambda a good fit, and why?
options: Yes, because 2 GB is within the limit
Yes, because Lambda has no time limit
No, because one call can run at most 15 minutes. Use a container task or split the job
No, because Lambda cannot use more than 128 MB
why: The memory is fine (up to 10,240 MB), but one Lambda call stops at 900 seconds. Read the limits before you pick Lambda.

q: Steady high traffic, 24 hours a day. Which bill shape usually gets expensive?
options: A right-sized always-on container
A rented server that is on all month
Per use, as with Lambda, where you pay for each call
None of them, the bill is always the same
why: At steady high load an always-on container is often cheaper, because you stop paying a premium per call. At low or spiky load, Lambda wins because nothing idles.
